The performance and capacity of neural networks beyond basic optimization also depend on their ability to memorize data and generalize predictions. Understanding this aspect is crucial as the dominant eigenvalue of the neural tangent kernel is linked to key regularization techniques and test-set behavior. This study focuses on quasi neural networks - subsets of neural networks constrained by their test data - and explores their eigenvalues and predictors. By analyzing their spectral properties, it is found that the test residuals of such networks continue to decrease and their test error can be precisely predicted and potentially bounded, offering insights into the capacity of neural networks beyond optimization. This research also extends to infinite-dimensional Gaussian process-like networks and may offer theoretical insights into similar networks with constrained initial inputs.

A requirement that a given entropy be minimal imposes constraints on corresponding bulk entropies, which in turn affect related entropy values within the system.  This characteristic is particularly relevant to understanding how entropy behaves in both the bulk and on the boundary of certain physical systems.  The minimality of entropy is a fundamental concept that is also embedded within certain versions of quantum information theory known as quantum information processing frameworks, which are based on specific algebraic structures, such as subfactors, quantum circuits, and von Neumann algebras.  This minimum entropy principle gives rise to certain relationships between the entropies of different systems, a concept known as monogamy of mutual information, within these frameworks.  Versions of this principle are also relevant to certain versions of gravity, such as holographic gravities.  This version of minimal entropy in holographic gravity is found to affect bulk entropy values.  The minimality of certain bulk entropy values leads to specific inequalities between competing geometric definitions of entropy values, which are also relevant to gravity theories that do not include a cosmological constant.  This concept is found to lead to a new inequality that relates how entropy behaves on both sides of a black hole event horizon, which is also relevant to another established relationship between entropy values known as the page-diagram inequality.  The concept that a given entropy be minimal appears to be a universal characteristic that defines how entropy behaves in certain versions of gravity, such as holographic gravities. The probabilities of local states in two perfectly integrable models of quantum models of matter is analyzed. The Hamiltonian of each model adheres to the symmetric tensor product of the fundamental permutation model, modified by a rational function of the gauge parameters. The model's partition function, when applied to a torus, yields matrix elements that belong to an irreducible representation of the symmetric group. By utilizing the quantum Kermack-McKendrick equation, key elements of the permutation group are calculated, ultimately enabling the derivation of local state probabilities through the application of the branching rule.

We investigated the signal recovery from one-bit measurements using an iterative approach that incorporates various stabilization techniques. We introduced a bit-flipping procedure designed for this purpose, then tested it against two other methods in an end-to-end framework, aiming to maximize transmission efficiency. We found that combining stabilization methods yields the best results, and our proposed method shows promising realism and effectiveness.

The primary objective of astronomical image addition, or coaddition, is to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio by combining multiple images of the same sky region. While linear coaddition algorithms successfully preserve point-source variability and maintain a consistent point-source shape, nonlinear methods (such as median and clipped-mean) are required to eliminate transient artifacts and cloudy pixels. However, these algorithms are ineffective for coadding images with varying point-source to pixel ratios or seeing conditions, resulting in distorted star shapes and flawed photometry. An experiment involving 200,000 stars from the SDSS data set revealed significant discrepancies in PSF profiles, introducing up to a factor of two error in magnitudes for point sources and giant stars, despite being negligible for intrinsic point source errors. To address this issue, an optimized algorithm was proposed, which is capable of maintaining consistent PSF profiles, uniform point-source shapes, and high signal-to-noise ratios, effectively addressing the issues associated with cross-talk and badly seeing-data.

We introduce a boundary version of Schramm–Loewner evolution that yields a stochastic process of chordal SLев processes along randomly varying curves. This innovative framework provides an accurate representation of imaginary surfaces first introduced by Angel and仙 Peng. Furthermore, our method establishes a connection between these surfaces and Liouville quantum gravity, incorporating a dynamically varying, continuously changing time parameter.

For the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with periodic boundary conditions, we establish that for any positive time value, the maximum norm of the velocity field is bounded above by the maximum velocity field norm at the start, provided that the velocity and pressure satisfy certain conditions of smoothness and that the velocity satisfies a specific condition of having a zero sum over the domain. These conditions are also sufficient for the velocity field to be smooth in time. Our proof involves showing that for any time, the velocity field can be expressed as a sum of the initial velocity and an integral involving a heat kernel and a nonlinear term related to the Navier-Stokes equations. We then use the properties of the heat kernel and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to show that the maximum norm of the velocity field is bounded above by the maximum velocity field norm at the start, provided that the velocity satisfies the specified condition of having a zero sum over the domain.

A single classical computer can verify multi-party computation in two steps: first it learns a function on encrypled inputs from candidates, then it checks if the result is correct on plaintext.  We have created a novel protocol for this verification process using conditional variable quantum computation circuits, allowing a single classical computer to verify multiple parties' inputs at once.  We have optimized this process by minimizing two-step interactions, allowing the verification to be performed in parallel.  The new protocol has an asymptotic speed advantage, performing verification in the same time it takes for humans to compare multiple numbers, and has a more efficient communication cost than existing protocols.  While there is a small overhead in calculation due to the quantum nature of the protocol, this can be compensated for with current experimental platforms.  Moreover, our research shows that the new protocol, like other protocols, is secure against quantum adversaries due to the application of random numbers.

Deep cell shape models learned from normal development can accelerate and enhance image analysis by generating synthetic time-lapse data for training unsupervised algorithms for image analysis, such as cell tracking and staining quantification. To our knowledge, there are no comprehensive comprehensive deep cell shape models that can facilitate this effect, so we establish a framework that constitutes a novel contribution. We create a dataset comprising fixed cellular morphologies from diverse regions in embryonic images and train a conditional adversarial network to compose embryonic time-lapse frames synthesis given tracking information. We evaluate our model through visual inspection of synthetic time-lapse frames and generate high-throughput lamellipodia imaging data for assessing model performance. Finally, we use the model to create synthetic time-lapse data for tracking unsupervised algorithms and compare their precision against real experimental data.

Researchers have long believed that the ability to identify enduring characteristics of an environment is crucial for agents to succeed in complex tasks. This assumption has difficult-to-test implications due to the inability to directly measure what constitutes a persistent feature and how often agents encounter them. A study designed a novel task for robots where this concept could be quantitatively evaluated using a statistical model. The results surprising revealed that while tasks were achievable, optimizing for frequent exposure to persistent features did not necessarily lead to better performance, and that the ability to integrate information over time was a crucial factor, contradicting the idea that learning about persistent features facilitates task completion.

A modified version of the Newtonian ECMC algorithm was created to address a issue where simulations of three-dimensional dipolar models stall in their dynamics. Models included simple and attached dipolar spin, as well as a more intricate scenario where ratios of magnetic to atomic stiffness remained constant during scaling tests. In addition to demonstrating that models could achieve faster dynamics through a new algorithm, the study focused on optimizing the number of attempted swaps to enhance efficiency. Notably, the analysis revealed that achieving the fastest dynamics required the number of attempted swaps to be either much greater, with a ratio around around around 10 to 20, than the number of actual executed swaps, with a ratio around around around 2 to 4, in contrast to previous estimates suggesting a ratio around around around 2 to 3. The study confirmed that achieving faster equilibrium sampling did not guarantee improved physical model dynamics. The analysis also showed that achieving faster dynamics did not always result in accurate representation of physical properties, with varying results depending on the specific model in question,.

One critical factor in developing successful sound event detection systems is the availability of up-to-date metadata. However, this information is often limited, resulting in suboptimal systems. To address this challenge, this study focuses on enhancing sound event detection data sets through temporal and frequency-based data augmentation techniques. By constructing a hierarchical environment with controlled randomness, this study aims to simulate various real-world conditions and expand the existing data set. The results indicate that environmental modeling through data augmentation can lead to significant performance improvements, with state-of-the-art results for the 2020 Deep Learning Working Group (DLEWG) challenge. The source code and ESRGAN ESD Data Set (ESED-SC) are available at https://github.com/mosch2000/ESED-SC.

We introduce a novel property known as superposition, enabling a multiple access channel (MAC) to combine multiple user messages into a unified output, a capability crucial for key aggregation in federated learning and for application in non-orthogonal multiple access systems.

First, we establish a superposition property, enabling the sum of multiple AWGN channel outputs to remain Gaussian, extending past research that showed individual AWGN channels produce jointly Gaussian outputs for common inputs.

Next, we leverage this superposition property to demonstrate the existence of a non-orthogonal multiple access scheme, facilitating increased spectral efficiency when users share a common file, with implications for federated learning and cryptography.

Finally, we extend this superposition property to include the encoder of a binary symmetric source through a binary sum, along with examples of superposition property applications, including a code construction similar to polar codes.

A novel approach to detection, estimation, and noise reduction in signals has been developed, utilizing an image processing concept known as level sets. Specifically, it utilizes spectrogram data, which is subset-based, to track and enhance signal features. By constructing a tree-like metric for similarity between time-frequency points, this method enables the tracking of evolving signal structures. It can accurately detect and refine discrete signal components by adapting to changing signal subsets, ultimately facilitating noise reduction and efficient parameter estimation for various signal types, including sinusoidal and impulse signals.

The equilibrium states, or clusters, of a balanced neural network can be accurately predicted through first-order asymptotic analysis. A system of balanced neural networks is characterized by dominant random excitatory connections and compensating inhibitory connections. By applying a unique and efficient method involving the intersection of eigenvalue hypersurfaces with the first-order spectrum, we can determine the existence and multiplicity of synchronized clusters. Our method also reveals the relationship between the parameters and variables of the network, allowing for control over the stability of the equilibrium states by adjusting the inhibitory parameter and synapse variance. Our findings demonstrate that beyond a certain critical point, the majority of the equilibrium states are stable.

We introduce a trained AI module that solves complex equations of motion for particles and clusters under various forces, including collision dynamics, without relying on pre-defined assumptions about the system's geometry or behavior. This module is based on a machine learning model called Physics-AE, which uses an advanced AI approach to transform traditional scientific methods into a comprehensive solution engine. By training it on random simulation data, it can learn to predict both the movement of individual particles and collective clusters. Its accuracy and general capability are confirmed through comparison with established scientific models and direct validation of simulation accuracy. The AI module significantly outperforms traditional methods by reducing computation time by a factor of 10,000.

Typically, quantum measurements are regarded as disruptive to thermodynamic processes that utilize thermal baths and external agents. Nevertheless, a specific type of ongoing quantum measurement known as weak measurement preserves coherence, leading to a unique thermal process. In contrast to standard measurement, this form of continuous quantum measurement treats the flow of information and heat between systems and their detectors/ environments continuously. We have developed a theoretical framework for analyzing systems undergoing continuous quantum measurement, focusing on heat and work associated with specific information content. Utilizing this framework, we investigate an information engine consisting of a two-level system and a continuous quantum information extractor that performs weak measurement. The results demonstrate that obtaining continuous information has a tangible heat cost and can be employed to perform useful work, highlighting a fundamental difference between discrete and continuous quantum measurement and broadening our understanding of information's thermodynamic implications in quantum systems.

We examined how a single disk, with varying weights, fills a confined space within a vertical, narrow container that is 10 units wide, necessitating the division into an upper, wider area and a lower, narrower section that is 10 times 3 units in size. We specifically focused on the point at which the disk, with a radius of about 1.6 units, first becomes trapped within the narrow portion. Due to the disk's elastic properties, it deforms when it comes into contact with the container's floor, introducing additional factors that affect its trapping behavior. We found that heavier disks, with weights greater than the force of gravity, tend to trap at a point closer to the narrow section, whereas lighter disks, with weights less than the force of gravity traverse the narrow section more efficiently. We support our findings with results from both simple calculations and a simulation that accurately accounts for the forces between the disk and the container's walls.

Research into the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle's impact on global precipitation reveals that El Niño, La Niña, and their unique variants, known as "flavors," exhibit distinct precipitation patterns. A study investigates how these distinct ENSO precipitation patterns affect a broad range of ecosystems, including snow-dependent systems, food security, disease spread, water management, cloud forest health, agriculture, monsoon behavior, and more. The findings suggest that these patterns can have significant societal and economic consequences, emphasizing the importance of accurate climate model predictions to aid community preparation and response. The study highlights the need to further explore the precipitation patterns' influence on diverse systems, along with the potential co-occurring atmospheric and oceanic changes that might independently affect these scenarios.

The development of an accurate understanding of the distribution and properties of supermassive black holes, as well as their formation and evolution, is a primary goal of the Vera Rubin Observatory and the James Webb Space Telescope. To achieve this goal, we conducted numerical simulations, using the ENZO code, of the merging of galaxies in a low-density cosmic environment, and we examined the growth of black holes that originated from the collapse of gas clouds or stars, as well as the addition of angular momentum during this process. The simulations revealed multiple pathways for supermassive black hole formation, and we found two distinct distributions in the spectral mass of these early black holes, corresponding to a range in the order of $10^{2-4.5}$ solar units and $10^{3.5-5}$ solar units, respectively. The initial masses and spins of these early black holes play a significant role in determining the eventual masses and distributions of black holes at a cosmological time of 13 billion years. By exploring various scenarios for early black hole formation, we found agreement with current observational data on the distribution and properties of quasar, although some fine-tuning of parameters is required in order to account for the observed variations in the spectral masses of early supermassive black holes, as well as the lack of detected gravitational waves detected by the LIGO-Virgo.

In this research, a correlation phenomenon associated with flat bands is examined within the framework of two-dimensional Hubbard models featuring multiple orbitals. Contrary to previous studies, which typically focus on square or triangular grids, we are examining a rhombic lattice where the flat bands emerge at the Fermi level. Our results, based on variational multicolor Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations, show that correlation effects associated with flat bands are pronounced when nearest-neighbor interactions dominate and the system exhibits a single Fermi surface. Moreover, the nature of these interactions is such that they foster magnetism in multi-orbital systems with p-d hopping connectivity. The study emphasizes the importance of rhombic lattice systems in understanding exotic phenomena within quantum materials, where geometric features significantly influence electronic behavior.

Understanding the underlying mechanisms of how the human genome's sequence determines trait development from a fundamental perspective is crucial for precision medicine. Research has not yet adequately addressed the question of how strongly sequence affects distinct traits. We developed a novel approach to quantify the impact of sequence on a specific trait by employing predictions from a deep learning model, PRO, which was used to perform a genome-wide association study on nearly 7000 association signals across 51 traits in the UK Biobank cohort. We found strong evidence that sequence has a greater effect on specific phenotypes via a genomic region's protein sequence rather than quantity, diversity of amino acids or other genomic features. We also discovered significant variation in sequence's influence across different traits but generally sequence's impact increases with greater computational complexity. These findings provide substantial evidence that sequence's influence on different specific phenotypes is primarily governed by the diversity of amino acids within a genomic region. This approach enables researchers to understand which regions are sensitive to sequence changes for each trait and how strongly sequence affects different specific phenotypes on a quantitative scale, providing a foundation for understanding complex trait mechanisms.

We establish that a 2-design with v being a prime power number of points possesses numerous structural characteristics, making it substantial that its automorphism group includes a prime p such that p is also the characteristic of its finite field.

We analyzed the Coulomb correlation energy in confined electronic systems using information theory. Current density functional theory lacks the ability to model Coulomb correlation effects in such systems. Researchers have shown that current density functional theory also can't accurately represent kinetic energy in these systems. In our investigation, the statistical nature of electronic wave functions and their relationship with local informational entropies in 1D and 2D confined systems were examined through both exact methods and numerical calculations. Current density functional theory's limitations in describing kinetic energy confirm the need for a correlation functional in the ground-state density approach that describes Coulomb correlation effects. We proposed specific requirements for the behavioral and statistical features of lateral kinetic energy densities, transverse kinetic energy densities, and their connection with parallel and lateral particle positions. The entropic connection between these quantities and their corresponding correlation energies was also explored.

Identifying wide binary star systems and gauging their dynamics over extended periods is crucial for understanding their nature and evolutionary patterns. This study focuses on analyzing one of these systems, consisting of stars H87 and H88, which is one of only a few with sufficient components for detailed spectroscopic analysis. Based on the available data, our team developed a novel graphical detection approach, using the full spectrum of each component, to measure their velocities with greater accuracy than one-dimensional methods. This significant improvement in precision allows for enhanced assessments of the system's properties and is implemented within the widely used BiWi algorithm for-wide binary detection and fitting. By applying our methodology to evaluate H87-H88, our findings reveal that the pair operates as a coherent, bound system with an estimated mass and periodic orbit. Comparing our results with previous studies, which considered only the primary component, we observed several discrepancies, which, according to our analysis, can be attributed to the inclusion of back-lighting effects from the giant disk surrounding H87. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of our graphically-based method, substantially improving the accuracy of wide binary star parameter measurements.

In multiplicative linear logic, a well-established link exists between the calculus multiplicative linear logic (MLL) and (MLL$I$)$\epsilon$, particularly through the use of (a normal form of) MLL combined with Com! and exponential rules that convey logical information through isomorphisms. Research has shown that MML$\epsilon$'s proof structures, specifically those that are normal, align with MLL's proof arguments, which in turn represent MLL's proof trees. Building on this knowledge, a new perspective is proposed, which relates MML$\epsilon$'s proof structures, an approach normal form, and MLL's proof trees. To establish this relationship, three key mechanisms are introduced: an initial step relating MML$\epsilon$'s proof structures, those that are normal and stratified, and MML$\epsilon$'s proof structures, which then relates stratified and confluence normal forms; next, the concept of ideal representations is explored, which connects MML$\epsilon$'s confluence normal forms with MML$\epsilon$'s proof trees; finally, ideal representations are related to MML$\epsilon$'s stratified normal forms through cut-free sharing graphs, which serve as an intermediate representation.

A critical challenge in the study of synchronized time series involves identifying which pairs are synchronized without prior knowledge. Traditionally, this challenge is addressed by assessing synchronization for each pair using a pre-defined metric, but this method is flawed as synchronization is an intrinsic property that cannot be quantified in isolation.  Instead,  a more appropriate approach would be for machine learning algorithms to automatically detect and predict which pairs are synchronized within an unknown system, based on established patterns.  However,  this issue has received little attention in the literature.  In order to address this gap,  a novel deep learning-based framework has been proposed, which enables the prediction of synchronization states for pairs of financial time series that have not yet occurred.  When tested on a collection of DFA-generated time series,  the model demonstrated exceptional accuracy in predicting synchronization, achieving a prediction accuracy of 92%.  Furthermore,  a correlation was found between the model's classification results and known characteristics of the time series, further validating its effectiveness.

The long-standing hypothesis that thermal fluctuations can facilitate barrierless reaction transitions has persisted for over a century. Recent theoretical and computational work has sought to provide evidence for this theory, but substantial doubts remain. We propose that targeting quantum states of vibrational modes in a reaction barrier, while coupled to thermal vibrations, may allow for barrierless management of the reaction process. By using quantum-stable vibrations as a guide for the reaction, we can access distinct nuclear configurations and increase the probability of achieving desired reaction outcomes, effectively making controlled chemical transformations more feasible.

Online advertisers seek to maximize their profits by monitoring key performance indicators, such as how many users click on their ads and how many subsequently make a purchase. With over 300 billion daily impressions and a daily traffic of 5 billion users on the internet, advertisers need efficient systems to accurately predict which users are most likely to click on their ads.  While modern deep learning-based advertising systems have achieved significant improvements, they are limited in their ability to utilize additional information about the interaction between ads and users.  A novel approach is proposed in this paper to utilize visual IDs, which capture visual patterns in user behavior, when training click-through rate (CTR) prediction models.  Experimental results show that training with visual IDs leads to significant gains in AUC (area under the curve) for CTR prediction when additional features are in place.  Furthermore, this information is highly transferable across different domains, with the ability to enhance the performance of models with limited data.

Business process models in enterprise IT typically aim for efficiency, flexibility, and cost-effectiveness, which can be restricted by control-flow constraints like those found in Petri nets, and sometimes by resource constraints.  Current resource management approaches enable various resource properties, such as resource types, assignments, and consumption patterns, to be checked during execution or pre-run analysis, but they lack support for concurrent activities influencing resource availability.

This paper expands the resource-sensitive model with support for multiple concurrent paths affecting resource usage and introduces an analytical technique called early detection.  The study differs from prior work in three key aspects - it accounts for cardinality constraints on concurrent activities, resources impacting concurrency, and activities only occurring when specific resources are present - an concept referred to as resource gating.  But as detecting all these properties may be an undecidable task, the paper instead develops a sufficient but not necessary detection technique, an approach that yields practical results in practice, and demonstrates that it does accurately identify properties for simpler process models lacking concurrent activities.

A new approach is developed to model and predict the air pollutant (aerosol optical depth) propagation from large forest fires across Europe. By combining observational data from AIRS satellite sensors with numerical models, we optimize model parameters to minimize errors relative to hyperspectral data. This parameter optimization is then utilized in a predictive numerical model of aerosol transport, informed by wilderness fire location data, to successfully forecast the air pollutant propagation and transport from forest fires. This approach successfully predicts and reconstructs wavelets originating from forest fires, with a prediction accuracy mean absolute error of 0.036 AOD through calibration. This accuracy allows for up to four-day predictions with reasonable accuracy through ongoing prediction extension, demonstrating the value and applicability of this air pollutant propagation modeling.

A significant issue with current location-based services (LBS) is the excessive location data collected by service providers, which poses a substantial privacy risk to users. While existing data collection methods reduce provider information, they often rely on inaccurate assumptions, such as using averages for independent data, or employ generalizations like cell tower areas, which fail to account for dependent data sources, potentially leading to a loss in analytical value. To address these limitations, this research introduces a novel analytical framework that precisely calculates data loss related to variance when sharing mobile location data with service providers. A specific method is detailed for handling data collected from grid cells. By accurately assessing data loss, this framework enables providers to determine appropriate security parameters for location privacy, thereby facilitating a better understanding of the trade-off between analytical utility and privacy protection.

Identifying individual characteristics and observing group variations within brain functional connectivity maps is crucial for understanding neurological diseases and brain development. However, the reliability of these comparisons is hindered by the phenomenon of inter-site effects, where differences between scanning sites influence connectivity measurements. This study investigates inter-site effects on functional connectivity and network configuration and its effect on the reliability of using functional connectivity maps to represent individual traits. Researchers addressed inter-site effects by standardizing connectivity maps using a site-specific robust multivariate regression and evaluated inter-site effects' impact on connectivity measurement reliability through an inter-site consistency metric. After standardizing, inter-site effects decreased from 57% to 35% for key neurological conditions and brain development-related scanning groups. Furthermore, inter-site effects decreased from 35% to 15% and 10% in explaining individual traits and group variations respectively post-standardization. Following this standardization process, inter-site effects were found not to significantly influence the inter-individual spread and group's brain functional network layout.

Cheatoms are nonabelian anyons in the second quantum Hall effect that follow statistics neither fully bosonic nor fermionic. A key feature of Cheatoms, derived from higher representations of Uq(su(2)), includes concentration of measure inequalities where the concentration depends on the deformation parameter q. We establish a link between these inequalities and the heat equation by utilizing a dynamic derived from the SU(2) group, leading to a concentration inequality of order q depending on the heat flow's time constant. Notably, this process relies solely on properties invariant under Markov dynamical processes, enabling its application to various systems such as quantum Markov chains and random walks on graphs, thereby generating concentration inequalities of order q for these systems based on their heat flow.

Despite code-switching's prevalence globally, current language models can't effectively process multilingual users, as they are limited to processing one language at a time. To overcome this barrier, we've developed an encoding method that treats languages as signals, enabling models to learn multiple languages simultaneously through a simple additional input. Experimental results on three tasks show our technique allows a base model to on par with, or even exceed, the performance of specialized single-language models, using zero-shot fine-tuning. Notably, it does not require model modifications or increased architecture complexity. Notably, we have released the code-switched English-Spanish Wikipedia dataset to facilitate further research at https://github.com/zensystem Ltd/cs-wiki.

To superconduct at high temperatures, unheated pressures of more than 150 GPa are required in H$_x$S. By applying first-principles calculations to find phonon spectra, our analysis indicates that isotopic substitution within the non-hydrogen components contributes a pressure-dependent effect that ranges from 0.5 meV/GPa at 150 GPa to over 3 meV/GPa at 250 GPa. This stands in contrast to prior estimates of 0.2 meV/400 GPa. Moreover, hydrogen isotopic substitution accounts for less than half the isotopic interaction within these compounds. Consequently, future research into superconducting materials with high critical temperatures should prioritize studying isotopic substitution within the non-hydrogen components.

Evolutionary searches for optimal solutions in nature rely on a strategy of replacing existing traits with incremental changes, using historical information, while disregarding overall significant changes, which occur on a much larger timescale. Evolutionary algorithms have long used a technique of substituting one component for another based on past success, however this approach risks replacing causal factors for key characteristics, which would require extensive genetic modifications, for minor features, which could mislead searches for optimal solutions. This risk is particularly prevalent in time-critical algorithms that require rapid response times. A new way of measuring the impact of changing a characteristic in a system has been proposed to better understand the relationships between substitutions and their effects, which could help guide evolutionary algorithms to avoid misleading improvements. A simulation using a difficult optimization problem has been used to test this new substitution metric and shown to be more robust than the traditional method, which measures the changes in optimization performance as a result of substitutions.

This research focuses on the role of closed-loop feedback in producing consistent, smooth walking patterns by testing several loop designs on a robotic platform. We initially examine the effects of delayed feedback during simulated motion, followed by evaluating multiple feedback types implemented on a physical robotic platform, the Hybrid Dynamical Systems Robot (HDSR). Delayed feedback highlights the challenges linked to predicting foot contact times. In contrast, event-based feedback triggers control actions based on real-time conditions. Threshold-based feedback utilizes a range of parameters to determine specific thresholds for control adjustments. All assessed strategies utilize a foundational control law modeling the robot's falling characteristics, but their implementations differ. Evaluation metrics included the success rate, smoothness, and consistency of produced walking motions, as well as the robustness of various feedback designs. Our findings indicate that delayed feedback results in inconsistent gait cycles, while closed-loop methods centered on triggering events at key points provide substantial improvements in walking smoothness and robustness.

We introduce a novel framework for camera pose estimation that utilizes multi-view descriptors. Traditional methods align features from multiple descriptors, resulting in inaccurate pose calculations for descriptors that don't have matching features. We propose a learning approach to automate alignment parameters for each descriptor, improving pose estimation in challenging situations. This framework is illustrated to enhance the performance of existing pipeline components, including deskew, feature extraction, alignment, and pose estimation. Extensive experiments are conducted on standard datasets to validate our approach.

In the context of federated learning, clients operate on local data and preserve its confidentiality, but this results in data heterogeneity. Furthermore, clients often have limited computing power, posing a challenge, especially for clients with less computational capacity. We observed that clients with more labels have greater potential to learn and contribute to the global model, thus enabling a personalized semi-supervised learning approach where clients without labels participate in fine-tuning, while clients with labels initiate the global model training. This balance in contribution allows the paradigm to tackle the data heterogeneity and labeling issue, and personalized learning. Experimental results on multiple image classification datasets confirm its effectiveness and practical value.

Following a neutron star's disruption in the accretion disk of a massive star, we observe the post-merger system's accretion disk evolution in numerical simulations. We specifically investigate the effect of magnetic fields in the accretion disk, which initially resides in the massive star, around a black hole. As we monitor magnetic energy growth, we measure the time it takes for a disrupted neutron star to fall into the black hole in relation to magnetic colapsar model predictions. Furthermore, we predict various phenomena arising from these magnetic fields, including months-long black hole X-ray luminosity, radio flares caused by particle jets, and potentially, short-gravity wave emissions.

For compact Riemann surfaces of genus $\gamma\geq 2$, we establish a maximum value for the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class in Jacobians, building upon Avner's previous work on Jeffery's last proposed class. This discovery also enables us to prove that Jeffery's conjecture for the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class is true for compact hyperbolic surfaces of genus $\gamma\geq 2$.

This study examines a specific Markov process that operates within a confined, bounded area of multi-dimensional space. Under distinct regularity conditions, we establish the existence of a single quasi-stationary distribution and provide evidence of consistent exponential convergence to this distribution, contingent on the process' paths and transition probabilities. Additionally, we establish bounds on the mortality rate function. These analytical findings are complemented by a detailed example of a markov process that includes a random walk component on a lattice within a bounded area of $d$-dimensional space.

Research has discovered a unique optical force behavior in graphene by utilizing its optoelectronic properties. Through experiments, it has been possible to utilize graphene's electro-optical adjustment to facilitate fine-tuning of optical forces acting on dielectric particles. By employing an optical tweezers system combined with electrical bias, the researchers achieved precise control over the equilibrium positions of dielectric particles. Furthermore, they explored the dynamics of particles under both passive and active forces, and computed the traversal times for particles moving from one position to another. Additionally, the researchers proposed a method to estimate the chemical potential of dielectric particles via current traversal times, and their findings have been validated through numerical simulations.

Patients in the Emergency Department (ED) who are awaiting treatment have a strong preference for shorter wait times, however, reducing this preference often comes with the risk of increased revisit, readmission, and treatment times. The objective of this study is to quantify the 30-day revisit, hospital admission, and average treatment time variations resulting from ED treatment time changes. By utilizing real-world data from over 10 million patient visits at two large EDs in Washington DC between 2012 and 2015, and 20 million patient visits across 400+ EDs in 2008, a regression analysis of discharge records was conducted, revealing the following outcomes for patients whose treatment time was extended by 30 minutes on the day of their ED visit: 1) a 3.12 percentage point (pp) increase in revisit rates, 2a hospital admission 0.44 pp increase, and 3) 11.1 minutes reduced average treatment time. The analysis also identified significant disparity patterns, with patient groups from certain demographic and background groups being more likely to experience revisit following an ED visit. Our findings offer valuable insights to policymakers, hospital administrators, and treatment time optimization model developers in balancing patient revisit and treatment time goals.

This research investigates how varying levels of task complexity influence task assignment in a multi-agent system, using a computational model. We examine a dynamic environment where agents make decentralized decisions on task execution, leading to an equilibrium outcome. This equilibrium provides a framework for mapping task difficulty to agent number. ToAn effective way of predicting task allocation in real-world settings, we developed a novel difficulty distribution model, drawing from an equilibrium concept, toBetter understand allocation patterns, we compared our framework's predictions with actual data from a controlled experiment and found a significant match, suggesting our understanding of task allocation is on the right track.

To accurately measure charge-dependent correlations originating from charge separation effects in heavy ion collisions, thorough background assessments are crucial. Researchers have developed high-precision calculations for the one-particle local conservation background and its impact on two-particle correlations with various charge pairs, considering the local conservation of protons, neutrons, and lambda particles. Furthermore, these calculations are extended to correlations incorporating local two-particle conserved quantities and the overall correlations after subtracting all conservation effects, calculated through a novel method called the N-triplet subtraction scheme. For marbles model simulations with varying parameters, the one-particle local conservation backgrounds overestimate correlation signals by an order of magnitude, making accurate accounting for these effects essential for correlators with signal-to-background ratios below 100. Two-method comparisons for removing the contributions of two-particle conserved quantities yield consistent results, with the direct subtraction of the two-point correlation function being slightly more precise than the event-by-event subtraction.

The analysis of crowd dynamics has been extensively conducted to identify the key attributes of crowd behavior, yet there's a notable lack of research applying this analysis to the fields of management and organizational sciences. A recent event, OpenSourceSummit's 2020 Indiegogo campaign, offered a unique opportunity to study crowd dynamics in a professional setting. Our study applied multi-level network analysis to data from the summit's campaign, creating three distinct graphs: one depicting project connections, another showing the relationship between projects and their creators, and a third outlining the contributions of creators. By comparing the analyzed features of crowd dynamics to other potential predictors, we identified significant connections between a project's network standing, its creator's characteristics, and fundraising success. Notably, the complexity of project networks showed a stronger correlation with fundraising amounts than the characteristics of projects themselves, while the amount a project received in funding was more closely predicted by the contributions of its creators, rather than the characteristics or popularity of those creators.

This paper presents an innovative fusion of federated learning and deep learning techniques for network intrusion detection. Traditionally, distributed ML models rely on a central server that collects all network data, compromising privacy. To address this issue, we developed a federated approach where a global model is created through collaboration among multiple organizations, each contributing local updates without sharing raw data. Furthermore, we utilized contrastive learning to overcome class imbalance problems present in network intrusion datasets. While existing federated methods suffer from communication efficiency and security concerns due to poisoning attacks, we introduced a new Poisson sampling based federated averaging algorithm. This algorithm limits the update frequency of participating institutions, thus improving communication and security without compromising accuracy. Experimental results using the KDD CUP 99 dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in advancing privacy-preserving and intelligent next-generation network intrusion detection systems.

In robotics, real-time decision-making is crucial due to limited processing power being spread across an expanding network of specialized algorithms. To tackle this challenge, we propose an learning method where decision-making agents acquire policies for specific tasks through reinforcement learning. These agents operate independently, using their personal memory of task requirements, thus reducing the computational load on the system, especially in the case of ongoing system tasks, as these agents can make decisions without system intervention. Our approach is evaluated in several widely recognized benchmark systems, where execution times decrease by as much as 40% due to system efficiency. Furthermore, we observe that these agents are capable of learning effective strategies that surpass the minimum required execution time by 15-20%.

The choice of semiconductor material is a key factor in determining the performance characteristics of a device, influencing its operating speed, power, and functionality, among other aspects. As new III-V semiconductor materials gain prominence due to their potential in data communication, thin film processing needs to be refined to enable their use in applications like data transmission and storage. We investigated how different gate materials affect the performance of nMOS thin film transistors made of n-type InGaAs and n-Channel GaN. By comparing the mobility of the semiconductor materials with their flat band voltages, our research reveals that mobility generally affects mobility voltage coefficient, and thus, a key transistor performance metric known as the inversion layer threshold voltage coefficient is affected by gate material. We utilized standard processing techniques, including alignment, for comparing the mobility voltage coefficient in both semiconductor types across different gate materials, and discovered significant variations in the mobility voltage coefficient depending on the mobility difference between the two semiconductor types. For n-Channel GaN, the mobility voltage coefficient correlates positively with the mobility difference, whereas for n-Channel InGaAs, the relationship is more complex due to the influence of other transistor parameters, such as substrate thickness and flat band voltage variations, on the mobility voltage coefficient.

The study focuses on the stability of time synchronization in populations of identical oscillators within a network structure, despite the presence of small discrepancies in their parameters. Using this analysis, the researcher calculates the likelihood of accurate timing for oscillators with randomly distributed parameters. It's also examined how this likelihood varies with the strength of connections between oscillators and whether the network is structured to have a specific pattern of connected groups or is merely random, with a given number of connections per oscillator. The results are then applied to understand the performance of complex systems, such as networks of fully connected synapses, cortical areas with specific connections, and even technologies like GPS, where the researcher confirms a specific distribution of timing errors among localized groups of oscillators.

This research examines whether popular Western search engines include covert promoting of specific services within their search results. Using a diverse set of search engines, the team tested the output for pre-written hidden texts, which would covertly promote specific services. A significant discovery emerged when searching from Google, Bing, and Yahoo! consistently included a hidden promotion of YouTube in their search outputs - in contrast, this phenomenon was absent in Baidu, Ecosia, and Baidu. Furthermore, content analysis revealed variations in the language used when promoting different services, with noticeable differences in grammar, vocabulary, and language structure across different search engines.

A rigorous mathematical framework is developed to handle the irregular behavior of flat connections around monodromy defects in curved surfaces. The theory diverges significantly from established regularization techniques that rely on local modifications. The dynamics of defects are captured comprehensively by the behavior of the Hurwitz zeta function. In a similar manner to non-defect systems, where the Frobenius manifold structure emerges through conformal scaling of geometric structures, the presence of a defect introduces a well-defined yet intricate interaction between this scaling mechanism and the monodromy, characterized by an infinite series expansion. The asymptotic behavior of this series as the exponent increases to a large positive value ensures the existence of a well-holomorphic interplay between scaling and monodromy, marking the limit in which long-range scaling dominates and allowing for a well-defined resolution of the defect through similarity transformation. The asymptotic behavior of the series also facilitates a well-holomorphic dependence on the monodromy, enabling a well-holomorphic dependence of defect solutions on the monodromy parameters. The solutions expressible through q-hypergeometric functions illustrate various examples. The derived formulas for all positive and negative integer exponents in the series expansion provide an alternative expression for all possible resonant solutions with distinct q-zeta function behavior for each resonant solution. The-13 equation, initially associated with modular elliptic curves, has been redefined for curves featuring a generic rational point on a cubic field extension, possessing order 13. We establish a classification for curves with this new-13 equation when the underlying rational field is either 1, 2, or 3. Our analysis also identifies the specific modular domains within the classically defined-13 equation, facilitating a more comprehensive understanding.
