This suggests that phonon excitations stabilize the helimagnetic phase and increase the helimagnetic gap. We also discovered that the magnitude of the helimagnetic gap is influenced by the lattice deformations, with implications for the magnitude of the transport anomalous Hall effect.

Recent advancements in Deep Neural Networks have significantly boosted the capabilities of NLP systems to interpret and analyze text, leading to improved performance of Relation Extraction techniques. This paper provides a comprehensive review of RE methods using DNNs in the last five years, focusing on the techniques of RE pre-processing, architecture choices, training methods, RE tasks, and evaluation metrics employed in DNN-based RE research. Additionally, it offers insights into the most frequently used datasets, published studies, and open problems in the field, ultimately suggesting potential research directions for the future.

We investigate the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for n-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$, focusing on domains composed of two balls separated by a hyperplane interface. The boundary conditions are mixed Steklov-Robin on the inner surfaces of both balls and continuity of the function across the outer equatorial boundary. By exploiting the problem's anti-symmetric properties, we reduce it to a boundary value problem on the upper hemisphere. Consequently, we analyze the influence of the two balls' radii and the Robin parameter on its first eigenvalue, particularly the critical Robin parameter above which eigenvalues exist and the decreasing trend of this critical value with increasing Robin parameter. Moreover, we examine the decay rate of this critical Robin parameter and provide numerical precision, along with expressions for the eigenvalue and critical Robin parameter for the limiting case as it approaches infinity.

Graph-based data representation and analysis have gained significant popularity in recent times, given that many real-world interactions can be effectively modeled as graphs, with nodes representing entities and edges linking them if they interact. As graph-based modeling has become increasingly popular, researchers have introduced the concept of hypergraphs to better capture multi-way interactions, given the fact that their general form is a two-dimensional projection of higher-dimensional data, similar to graphs and matrices. Since graph-based analysis tools have been well-established, there has been a surge in interest among researchers to develop new methods for hypergraph construction and information extraction from their projections. This area of research is critical, considering the vast amount of multi-way interaction data that can be analyzed using hypergraphs, such as two-party interactions in graphs and the connections between party ID, votes, and candidate IDs in contemporary US elections. Through the application of hypergraph analysis tools to real-world data, we demonstrate that hypergraphs outperform graphs, networks, and other data representations in accurately representing data and can be optimized for specific tasks, such as clustering, by leveraging both local and global properties of their projections. The results also highlight the significance of multi-way interactions in understanding data, as they can be utilized to enhance clustering results in noisy data and result in more interpretable clusters. The code for our method is available on our GitHub page.

PAXRay is a large, detailed dataset of 2020 signed X-ray reports in multiple formats, featuring precise spatial positioning for highlighted image regions. These spatial annotations facilitate visual grounding tasks on X-ray images by linking report segments to specific image areas. We analyzed the quality of these annotations from a radiologist's perspective and explored the effectiveness of different radiological report segments for visual grounding tasks. Experimental results showed that patient-specific information enhances learning, while removing information gradually also improves task performance. Moreover, a simple, effective method was found to successfully train X-ray visual grounding using only text input. Finally, the PAXRay dataset and tools are made publicly available to support further research advancements.

This article presents three sets of surfaces containing explicit examples that demonstrate counterparts to prior results in Euler class theory for foliations. Firstly, one set consists of surfaces where every integral second cohomology class, with a norm of one, can be realized as the Euler class of a foliation, providing counterexamples to the proposed theorem. Secondly, a set of surfaces is identified where the second cohomology class with the minimal norm achieved by a foliation's Euler class is not one, also countering Brumfiel's proposed conjecture. Moreover, a set of surfaces is demonstrated where this minimal norm is unbounded as the norm of the Euler class increases, further illustrating discrepancies. Additionally, methods are outlined for deriving various invariants of foliations from a given vector field on the surface, enabling explicit constructions.

This study explores the concept of directional non-directional emission using a simple experimental setup, employing either a diode laser or an optical resonator made from tape. By varying the divergence angle between two flat surfaces, specific divergence nodes emerge where emission is predominantly directed, rather than being isotropic. When these nodes appear, up to a 30-fold increase in directionality is observed in full-width-at-half-maximum measurements. By examining the divergence nodes across six spectral ranges utilizing single-energy emissions and white light, we reveal that divergence rather than isolation of vertical horizontal coupling responsible for this phenomenon. To further understand directional non-directional emission, we propose a model emphasizing reservoir mode depletion and the inherent randomness of spontaneous emission, ensuring reproducible results.

This research examines the interconnections between ten prominent cryptocurrencies - Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, Ripple, Monero, IOTA, Cardano, VeChain, BNB and Algorand - from January 2020 to January 2021. A weekly analysis was performed using log returns and Spearman's rank, revealing a significant year-over-year rise in correlations during the first six months of our study period. Notably, the correlations YTD in January 2021 surpassed the YTD correlations in 2019 by a substantial margin, suggesting a heightened level of risk among these cryptocurrencies.

A theoretical framework is developed for analyzing the highly nonlinear hydrodynamic behaviors described by the KPZ equation under minimal noise conditions, complementing existing simulations. A novel perturbation theory is developed within this context, estimating the noise-influenced transformation between reference frames with varying densities. Through this approach, we derive an expression for the noise's impact on density fluctuation growth rates, which aligns with prior research within its limits of applicability.

To study solar wind turbulence at close distances, the need arises for mass-independent plasma potential probes, robust against contamination. Comparing the capabilities of JP1 and LSP measurements in identifying turbulence spectra, we utilize 1 AU solar wind data from March 2014. Although JP1 and spacecraft potential measurements yield similar spectral results, slight discrepancies arise, particularly affecting the spectra at high frequency end. Furthermore, VP estimates tend to produce inaccurate spectra when the signal-to-noise ratio is low, underscoring the significance of utilizing high signal-to-noise ratios to obtain accurate spectral results, an aspect often overlooked.

The gap-mode of oscillating X-ray free-electron lasers (GAXR FELs) holds great promise for producing intricate, multi-dimensional coherent light. Employing chirp-taper and feedback mechanisms, researchers can optimize GAXR FEL processes, yielding ultra-brief pulses in EUV and soft X-ray spectra. This study delves into the effects of these processes on the generation of such pulses. Through detailed simulations, findings indicate that a well-calibrated FEL amplifier can generate a 3-fs pulse with 600 mJ energy at 1.4 nm wavelength, leveraging a combination of chirp, energy extraction, and re-bunching energy restoration. This is accomplished with a pair of chirped undulators in a gap-mode undulator, offering improved performance. Furthermore, results show that a minimal gain length is essential for achieving high peak power on the order of kW.

The modified Taylor-Goldstein equation differs from the classical inviscid equation by transforming the fourth-order vertical velocity perturbation equation into a more comprehensive 6x6 matrix form. This new equation takes into account both vertical and horizontal velocity perturbations. By utilizing an ansatz approach with a solution in terms of six solution vectors and corresponding frequencies, the equation can be thoroughly analyzed. The resulting frequencies are solved via a non-linear eigenvalue problem which is ultimately represented as a generalized eigenvalue problem. The eigenvalues were calculated for a specific case of smooth background wind profile using the least squares method. The results are compared to inviscid instability modes and found to be in agreement, additionally the instability modes have also been confirmed to converge. The study's results have potential applications in atmospheric and oceanic sciences.

Creating fair electoral districts is essential, yet subject to varying notions of fairness. To better evaluate districting plan fairness, we propose an approach that treats districting as an optimization issue. By utilizing Simulated Annealing, even novice facilitators can efficiently explore a vast number of possible plans. The resulting collection of alternatives enables a more nuanced evaluation of fairness, allowing stakeholders to make more informed decisions. This method was put to test in multiple mock redistricting competitions, demonstrating Simulated Annealing's ability to generate a diverse set of plausible alternatives and enhance stakeholder engagement in real-world democratic processes.

A novel approach based on matrix decomposition is proposed to address the challenge of fabric defect detection, which has historically been limited by the necessity for precise positioning of samples to filter out irrelevant background details. By utilizing singular value decomposition, the intensity of the image can be separated from the defect data, thereby eliminating the need for sample alignment. To optimize computational efficiency, grouping of pixels and multi-scale analysis are employed, and results are combined to minimize the occurrence of false defects. Experimental results on high-moisture silk and polyester fabrics demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, achieving a detection rate of 98.8% on 100 silk defects smaller than 5 mm, without manually positioning the fabric.

This note outlines a performance assessment for visual reinforcement learning-based agents, proposing new learning objectives that promote exploration, based on mutual information calculations between actions taken and observations made, and also puts forward action-based and cross-modal entropy objectives for reinforcement learning, with a focus on reinforcement learning from random start points and offers suggestions for improved evaluation methods.

Building on previous research by Clément and Tourrencie (2021), I examine how matter behaves in Brans-Dicke theory when matter is conformally coupled. I demonstrate that, if a configuration of matter is capable of producing scalar gravitational radiation, and if the associated photons can escape to infinity, then those photons would carry away energy, which contradicts the assumptions of the model. Consequently, it is concluded that, in order for photon escape to occur, photon radiation must also be present, and no energy loss of the matter sector occurs. I also iterate that this conclusion holds true regardless of the specific form of the matter, and I look at two particular instances: one, a scalar field, and two, a Kerr black hole surrounded by photons. I find that, in both instances, photon escape results in no net energy loss.

We've studied the merger rates of stellar mass black holes formed from Population III stars within the cosmic web. Using a state-of-the-art code, GCUBED, we've tracked how often Pop III stars merge and how their remnant binaries evolve. GCUBED accurately models the formation of galaxies from the top-down, accounting for how Pop III stars are distributed across the cosmic web. We've analyzed two scenarios, varying the Pop III star formation rate, and found that mergers of single stars peak at high redshifts (z = 9-10), while those of binaries and their remnants peak at even higher redshifts (z = 7-8). Our findings suggest a specific rate of mergers (black holes per cubic gigaparsec per year), peaking at a rate of around 0.07-0.09.

Incident detection in distribution grids with frequent modifications and unknown parameters remains a significant challenge, primarily due to the lack of effective modeling parameters. Data-driven techniques have shown potential in improving detection rates, but converting them to residual generation is often difficult without accurate parameters, especially for post-conversion mapping. This study investigates the use of predictive control techniques to carry out data-driven residual calculation and defines a new loss function for residual estimation without needing parameters. Two concepts are introduced to calculate the total error between predicted and measured data within a specific time frame, leading to two formulations for generating residuals without requiring parameters. These formulations are compared, and it is found that one formulation converges to the desired residual without parameters, while ensuring the predicted data remains bounded. This convergence also ensures that these bounded values reflect actual system events. Furthermore, the results indicate that reducing the prediction horizon leads to improved convergence rate and enables the identification of an optimal prediction horizon that ensures boundedness while minimizing errors within a specified error threshold. These findings are supported through simulation results, which demonstrate the improved performance of a data-driven incipient detection algorithm.

To determine the individual effects of the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons, as well as their $C$-forbidden counterparts, in the final states of $X(3872)\to J/\psi\pi\pi\gamma$, we used spectral analysis to separate their contributions in experiments by LEPS and LHCb. Under the assumption that only $\omega$ and $\rho$ resonance contributions are present, our analysis of the azimuthal angle distributions suggests a significant difference in the relative contributions of these two mesons, with $\vert A_{\omega}\vert^2/\vert A_{\rho}\vert^2$ being less than one over, equal to, or less than one under. Furthermore, we found that the relative phase between the $\omega$ and $\rho$ amplitudes is approximately $180^\circ$, consistent with previous studies. When considering the transverse and longitudinal components of the $\omega$ and $\rho$ amplitudes, the ratio of their relative phases was found to significantly deviate from $180^\circ$, although the uncertainty associated with this measurement is relatively large.

Building on previous work, we establish the smooth quadrics in a projective space over a field of characteristic 0 are adequately characterized by their bordered Hirschowitz invariants. Characteristic 2 presents challenges; while quadrics and their cohomology theory are well understood, we develop a distinct approach for bordered Hirschowitz invariants. Additionally, we explore the impact of the fields' characteristic on low-degree smooth quadric geometry.

TextWorlds are text-based environments that are well-suited for training agents to conduct sequential decisions, however, existing simulations are too slow for large-scale trials. Our innovation, TextWorldExpress, overcomes this limitation by providing a high-performance Python library for interactive simulations of TextWorlds, enabling faster exploration and experimentation. TextWorlds simulate virtual worlds through domain-independent tasks that are complex, interactive, and potentially infinite in duration. In our testing, we verified the accuracy of TextWorlds simulations using TextWorldExpress against the original implementations, revealing a 700 times speedup (approximately 2 to 4 hours vs. 5 minutes) for a long-term task. This speed enhancement facilitates widespread adoption of TextWorlds simulations, empowering researchers to simulate and evaluate a vast number of text-based game environments efficiently. TextWorlds simulations are now freely available on the textworld.org website.

In the study of three-dimensional Topological Insulators, typically robust against disorder, the impact of specific types of defects on electron flow is not thoroughly understood. This study focuses on the effects of line defects on the transport of electrons within three-dimensional Topological Insulators, incorporating both numerical simulations and analytical findings. A key outcome of this research is the discovery that electrons can traverse these defects with considerable probability, despite the presence of disorder, due to nodes that develop as a result of interactions between electrons and defects. This phenomenon occurs specifically in certain orientations of defects and can lead to enhanced electron propagation. Furthermore, an analysis of the surfaces of these Topological Insulators indicates that electrons can also bypass defects, passing through the material's boundaries and potentially increasing their conductance. This surface effect becomes more pronounced as the level of disorder in the bulk increases and can account for the observed experimental data, offering a new explanation for the unexpected increase in conductance in Indium Antimonoxide samples.

We investigate positive $p$-harmonic functions on a family of non-subinhitive cones in $\mathbb{R}^N$, examining how the parameter $p$ affects uniqueness. Specifically, we demonstrate that when the parameter $p$ exceeds a certain threshold determined by $N$ and the cone's geometry, uniqueness fails due to the existence of non-trivial limit functions at infinity. Conversely, when uniqueness fails for all gradients, we demonstrate that it is also failed for all $p$-values. Furthermore, when this threshold is not exceeded, we establish a crucial connection between the set of harmonic functions on such a cone and the space of polynomials defined on the cone's cross-sectional manifold, highlighting the significance of polynomial functions in this context.

This research investigates Extremal Spatio-Temporal Dependence using wind speed and wave height Metop data from the European remote sensing platform. Employing a reverse invariance principle and extremal transform, we map spatial configurations of extreme events within a single time period to joint distributions, allowing for time-independent, asymptotically spacetime-invariant models. These transformed joint distributions are analyzed through nodal chains, providing crucial insights into rare co-occurrences of extreme event configurations. Focusing on Metop data, we demonstrate that conditional extremal spatial dependence decays exponentially at a rate of approximately 1500 km for wind speed and 250 km for wave height. Furthermore, this dependence's rate is influenced by extreme event magnitudes, increasing as MLE values for these parameters rise.

This study investigates a hyperbolic concept introduced by Friedberg, and proposes an analogy between the criteria for point existence on variety sub-loci and the principles of hyperbolicity. To support this hypothesis, we present two key findings: first, we establish a hyperbolic property for the Jacobian of a curve defined over a function field; second, we explore the hyperbolic characteristics of certain abelian surfaces, and apply these results to examine the existence of rational points without relying on the Generalized Abelian Langlands Correspondence or the hypotheses of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture.

A novel approach to represent manipulability matrices or ellipsoids is introduced 
within this research, grounded on the concept of Riemannian manifolds. Various 
different manifolds are compared, with an examination of their properties 
and a suggestion for an optimal choice. Additionally, a method is proposed 
for calculating manipulability indices, and the concept of comparing shapes 
using geodesic distances is extended to ellipsoids. This enables a way to 
represent the orientation and eccentricity of under-actuated shapes based on 
over-actuated shapes' geodesic distances. Lastly, the practical utility of these 
manifolds is demonstrated through various numerical studies on robots with 
variable distances, such as cables and springs.

This paper presents an advanced approach for optimizing Higgs boson signal detection across multiple channels by addressing the issue of top quark pair background across various energy levels. A machine learning technique is employed to classify top quark pair events into distinct categories, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of the ATLAS detector. Eight alternative top quark pair classifications are developed using two datasets from the ATLAS detector, thereby improving the detection of the Higgs boson signal. Eight corresponding analysis regions are optimized for each channel using a multi-objective genetic algorithm, thereby maximizing the discovery potential of the Higgs boson across the eight channels. Eight discovery significances are calculated for each channel, revealing improvements of up to 13% over the standard analysis regions. Seven of the eight channels showed reductions in the required luminosity of up to 11%, with the eighth showing a 4% reduction. An additional 3% luminoosity savings is achieved through a data-driven method known as pseudo-likelihood, which combines the likelihoods of the top quark pair classifications for each channel.

The performance of most 3D object estimation models is heavily dependent on the quality of the canonical pose dataset used for training. This paper presents a novel method to learn canonical poses across various categories of objects in a single framework by leveraging the extensive data from multi-stage training. We initially learn to transform images into 3D shapes at various poses, and then develop an internal database to transform these volumes into canonical forms by refining the outer shape and aligning categories. Surprisingly, incorporating this method into existing deep learning-based object estimation models resulted in significant improvements in performance, and we were able to generalize this technique to scenes and molecules with great success. The proposed method and the associated database are available on the project's GitHub page.

Our primary objective is to explore vaccine-related misinformation's influence on public mindset. To achieve this, we created a comprehensive framework for extracting and analyzing personal beliefs from social media text content. By leveraging a pre-trained language model, our system identifies and categorizes individuals' stance on specific claims, which we then analyze to draw meaningful conclusions. We apply this framework to 466,255 Twitter posts regarding five prominent COVID-19 vaccines, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in tracking disseminators' narrative strategies and changing public perception over time. Additionally, we demonstrate its ability to uncover subtle connections between different concepts.

The rapid field oscillations in attosecond pulses are controlled through a cutoff radius, which also determines the pulse's initial phase, scarce data until now. We demonstrated this phase dependence using infrared fields as a cutoff variable in HHG simulations, revealing how adjusting the cutoff radius allows fine-tuning of both energy and duration. Furthermore, utilizing non-circular orbits at the cutoff radius led to the generation of chiral attosecond pulses with isolated sub-angstrom helical wavefront curvature, potentially enabling sub-angstrom transverse temporal resolution.

The reliability of the 7h 56m 15s Algol C orbital period, first established by ancient Babylonian astronomers over 2,000 years ago, has been scrutinized using a multitude of different observation methods.  Researchers have analyzed the data and discovered significant deviations from this period, all of which have been plotted for comprehensive visualization.  Excluding the original Babylonian and classical observations, which span nearly two millennia, 21 different time scales have been carefully calculated.  The findings suggest that the remaining observations have led to a varying orbital period since the initial determination.  Consequently, the original Algol C period has been adjusted to account for these adjustments resulting in an adjusted time period extending back over 2,000 years.  The best representation of this adjusted period has been achieved through the utilization of the LT3 time scale and reveals a constant decrease in the orbital period at a rate of 3:28:00/century.  The degree of contribution that the Babylonian observations make to this constant decrease varies heavily depending on whether they are included in the analysis or not and remains uncertain.

We investigate the non-linear Schrödinger equation within a bounded domain of R^3, and derive an example of a wave function that exhibits a sudden collapse at the boundary within a finite time, different from the original method by Merle, Veereman and Kenig, Tanaka.

Physics-informed neural networks have emerged as promising tools for resolving complex partial differential equations, yet they face significant limitations when applied to complex problems, primarily due to their dependence on network architecture and the need for extensive data. In an effort to overcome these obstacles, we introduce an innovative approach, the Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG), which dynamically adds nodes to the training set in response to residual errors. By generating novel nodes only where and when needed, RANG enables faster convergence and reduces computational costs. RANG comes in two variants - one incorporating a K-means clustering process to identify novel nodes, and another employing a kernel-based method to directly adapt the residual-weighted integral. RANG's effectiveness is showcased across multiple benchmark problems, with consistent improvements in performance and efficiency.

Our study is centered around the development of a computational framework for analyzing the transmission capabilities of gate-optimized ferroelectric field-effect transistors within a six-terminal device model. To simulate the interaction between electrons and the ferroelectric material's domain structure, which exhibits a periodic arrangement of alternating polar orientations up or down, we have implemented a novel ab initio approach. This involves transforming the first-principles calculation into real space k-space grids, which enables the accurate replication of the texture-induced periodic potential in the conduction bands. Furthermore, we have formulated a multi-domain device model incorporating this periodic potential, allowing for a comprehensive simulation of the carrier transport in the gate-optimized FeFET. This model incorporates not only the texture-induced periodic potential but also the domains' separate work functions. To simulate the electric field-driven domain switch, which influences the work function and conduction profile, we have developed a coupled Poisson equation system and introduced a mobile electron density model for optimizing the gate voltage. This enables the accurate prediction of the field-driven domain switch based on the induced electric field in the gate dielectric. Finally, through extensive transmission studies, we have obtained detailed insights into the ferroelectric material's transmission spectrum and the corresponding impacts on the operation of these transistors.

Cargo, a package manager for the Rust language, manages a vast repository of over 1,500 library dependencies used by more than 2,000 funded projects. A study analyzed the security of its code by testing 337 popular libraries used in the cargo test data set against the SCAR-O vulnerability oracle, which is based on 1,500+ CVEs. These libraries totalled 4,745 lines of public and private code. A study revealed that nearly 70% of their code contains security vulnerabilities, with 37% still vulnerable in their latest versions. Furthermore, study found that code similarity is a key factor in the spread of these flaws, causing the share of affected dependencies to rise from 15% to 47%. A study also suggested that the open source community can effectively mitigate these risks by updating libraries and utilizing code-sharing methods such as the copy-and-interpret technique.

This study examines the ergodic behavior of stochastic complex equations on a confined domain with the condition that boundary values are kept constant. These equations model systems influenced by random events that cause abrupt changes, known as pure jump noise, and with the intensity of noise that depends on the system's state. When no system-dependent limitation exists, these equations can be thought of as modeling systems influenced by compound Poisson events. Under the condition of low external input, we show that these equations possess a unique stationary distribution, even in scenarios where the equations involve complex systems with multiple components and with the equations' mathematical structure limited in extent. Additionally, we establish the rate at which these equations converge to their stationary distributions by considering both situations in which the equations are and are not subject to system-dependent limitations.

For non-cyclic abelian groups, the power graph of a group G is defined by connecting the vertices representing the elements of G, where an edge exists between vertices a and b if a is the power of b or b is the power of a. Researchers have proposed potential power graphs by removing edges related to the minimal degree subgroups when the group G meets specific criteria, but this work aims to determine the precise degree for the potential power graphs of finite non-cyclic abelian groups. By doing so, it will confirm the potential power graphs' degree for the specified groups, and will also allow for the calculation of the exact degree when G is a finite non-cyclic abelian group of a particular type.

Measurements taken at the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings with a Q-meter are being compared to theoretical predictions from quantum electrodynamics (QED) for laser backscatter. These measurements, although made at energies lower than what the Large Hadron Collider reaches, demonstrate the accuracy of the classical spin parameter in the classic energy range. When combined with the validity of the classical spin parameter at lower energies, as documented in an earlier document, these findings support the implementation of spin parameters at lower energies within the framework of the classic equation of motion.

This paper introduces a sophisticated image processing technique, Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which integrates Gabor features with SIFT keypoint refinement for robust image representation. SIFT keypoints ensure consistency across scale and rotation changes, but their limited scope hinders optimal structure capture. Additionally, they may be affected to large rotational discrepancies. LGFs leverage RBF-refined SIFT keypoints to define lens-shaped LGF units for robust feature extraction. Each unit combines morphological refinement with Gabor filtering for robust feature creation. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate LGF enhancement for robust image recognition against orientation changes. Subsequent experiments explore the application of LGFs for image classification and deep network pre-training, achieving SIFT-discriminative performance for the EbM-NUSCenes dataset in a novel cross-domain 3D object orientation estimation task.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved significant success in solving various graph-related problems. However, GCNs are often hindered by issues of overfitting and slow training and inference in sequential computation. Recent research indicates that GCN node features are highly sparse, suggesting the potential of out-of-order execution techniques to optimize computation. Unfortunately, the order of fetching node features in GCNs disrupts cache locality, rendering existing techniques inapplicable. To address this challenge, we propose Computation-Oriented Graph Feature Gathering with Predictive Pre-fetching (COGGaPP), a novel framework for integrating predictive pre-fetching into GCNs. COGGaPP predicts which nodes will be required in future layers of the GCN graph convolutional network, allowing for out-of-order fetching of these nodes' features. COGGaPP also incorporates an edge-directed feature aggregation mechanism and maintains an edge-directed load address queue for load-to-register operations. Our pre-fetcher utilizes an k-Nearest Neighbor algorithm, enabling a significant reduction in computational processes by up to 40.8% compared to state-of-the-art GCNs.

Recent research on Trojan attacks on neural networks has revealed their vulnerability in embedded systems, yet many NNS Trojan sources of failure are difficult to replicate in hardware. Unlike previous studies, which utilize Tinney et al.'s method but encounter implementation challenges, this research successfully applies a valid Trojan attack in hardware. The proposed attack in this study successfully triggers on FPGA, allowing it to deceive both white-box and black-box attackers while maintaining the original network's performance until a specific input condition is met. Furthermore, the proposed attack can be applied to various hardware platforms, including FPGA, ASIC, and SSOC, rendering it highly practical in real-world scenarios. The proposed attack has been empirically validated using the CIFAR-10 network, demonstrating a notable enhancement in both trigger rate and accuracy compared to previous attacks. The proposed attack's effectiveness remains comparable even under adversarial attacks such as PGD. The proposed attack's code is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Guopenghang/Tinney-RealHardware.

ROSIE IFU, a groundbreaking instrument, will integrate 36 individual wide-field fields of view to precisely track the spatial distribution and chemical composition of vast, distant celestial objects, such as nebulae, galaxies, and the intergalactic medium, across the entire object at H$\alpha$ and key related wavelengths in the range of 4.91-5.35 $\mu$m. These fields will be arranged in a hexagonal pattern, with each view having a 12 arcsecond pixel field, totaling a 70 arcsecond field. By utilizing IFU technology, ROSIE IFU, a planned 30cm space-based observatory, will provide high-quality data, significantly expanding upon current 2D spectral capabilities in the JWST range. Although primarily aimed at studying the Very Low Mass Intergalactic Medium, its 6 separate modes can study a broad range of celestial objects such as exoplanets, nebulae, galaxies, and the celestial medium, including the JWST range.

A comprehensive knowledge of low-energy fusion, specifically the $J$-factor, is essential for astrophysicians to comprehend various stellar phenomena, including the stability of the red giant branch, the dynamics of the horizontal branch, the evolution of asymptotic giant branches, the production of light elements through the $CNO$ cycle, the creation of metal in stars, and the enrichment of the interstellar medium with p-nuclei. To gather this information, the ERDA held a workshop at the Institute for Nuclear Theory in September 2004, where participants from astrophysics, nuclear physics, and accelerator physics exchanged research findings and discussed future collaborations. This workshop series continued with another event held at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in October 2005. The discussions from both events were published in two published volumes focusing on astrophysical $S$-factor factors, nuclear reaction rates, and accelerator beam targets, respectively. With the participation of research scientists from ERDA, the joint meeting of nuclear and astrophysical research scientists was held at the California Institute of Technology in October 2007, where a discussion on astrophysical $S$-factor factors was conducted. This workshop series continued with the 7th ERDA Astrophysics, Nuclear Physics, and Accelerator Beam Technology workshop.

Researchers find and analyze 126 exoplanets orbiting seven Sun-like stars with high frequency, each with a habitable zone orbit distance of around 0.1-0.3 AU. Most of these planets are smaller than or equal to Earth in size, resembling Venus, Mars, or Earth. Planets discovered in this study fall within the categories of Super-Mercury, Mars-sized planets, Earth-sized planets, and Super-Earths. A significant fraction of these planets are located within the habitable zones of their host stars, similar to Earth's position. However, planets found in this research are more likely to be more massive and have different compositions of ices and volatiles compared to Earth. It's crucial to characterize these planets through spectroscopy to learn about their atmospheres and surface  atmospheres. If the planets discovered in this research don't have atmospheres or have minimal atmospheres, they can serve as useful comparisons for analyzing the atmospheres of Earth-like planets in other habitable zones, such as TRAPPIST-d.

This paper proposes a novel attention-based massive MIMO system which incorporates
attention mechanisms for channel state information feature learning and data
transmission. By utilizing attention, we enhance the learning capabilities of
Channel State Information in adaptive and secure feature acquisition. Further,
ch'effect of attention brings about adaptive modulation, coherent transmission
and coherent reporting. The experimental results reveal that attention yields
better learning outcomes and signifies a pivotal role in channel reporting. A
efficient feature learning method based on CSE with Attention is developed which
exceeds the existing LSE-based comparative method in terms of accuracy. In addition,
this research yields better link adaptation and secret-key generation results. The
proposed approach relies on deep learning, specifically Long Short-Term Memory
(LSTM) with Attention, which outperforms the existing CSP-based approach with
Attention and LSTM, especially in terms of adaptation rate and generation rate.

This study introduces a comprehensive set of rules for constructing modern semantics for modal logic by leveraging topological categories and exploring their relationships with functor semantics. We recommend redefining Eesp as a generic term for topological semantics and functor semantics as a specialized form. The proposed unified framework allows for direct generalization of key theoretical concepts, including completeness theorems, Brouwerian theorems, and Smullyan theorems across various modal logic extensions. Additionally, this framework facilitates seamless translation of modern semantics methods into abstract semantics, further broadening its applicability.

The $\varnothing$-chromatic number $\vartheta(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the minimum number of colors needed for a specific type of graph coloring, where adjacent vertices must have colors separated by an edge. In 1990, Rubin proposed that every graph with a maximum degree of 3 can be colored using 5 colors such that the distance between any two vertices colored with different colors is at least an edge. This conjecture was proven false when Král' et al. found infinitely many bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 requiring 5 colors, but they required some edges have a maximum degree of 5. We establish that if we limit the edges with a high degree to be localized around a small set of vertices, then infinitely many such bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 would still need 5 colors for the $\vartheta$-coloring, confirming the 5-color version of the conjecture for graphs with limited edges, where the maximum degree is 5.

The minimal support size for $f$ in eigenspaces $V_m$ of Hamming graphs $(q,i,n)$ is studied, where each vertex is connected to $i$ other vertices through edges to elements from a fixed set of $q$ labels. For specific scenarios, the smallest support size for $f$ in $V_m$ has been proven to be $\binom{n}{m}(q-1)^{1/2}(n-2i+q-1)^{\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}m}$. In other situations, the smallest support size follows a similar pattern but replaces $q-1$ with $q-i-1$ in the expression, where each support size is also divisible by $(q-i-1)/2$. Additionally, this research investigates Crisman's conjecture stating that for a specific scenario, the minimal support size for $f$ in $V_m$ adheres to a specific inequality and provides a proof of the conjecture. Furthermore, some Eisenbud-Tseng bounds are also considered.

This report details how to integrate and use the COPASI systems biology modeler within Python applications, leveraging PySB's compatibility with COPASI. We outline the steps to employ COPASI and PySB within Python, highlighting COPASI's command-line functionality and the advantages of using both libraries. Furthermore, we describe a extension, ShinyCOPASI, that enables interactive modeling using RMarkdown with shiny.showcopasi(). This tool facilitates model visualization and analysis within a web interface, providing access to COPASI features alongside shiny ecosystem capabilities.

Achieving consistency between data collected from various sources and/or formats is crucial for data integration and analysis. Achieving this goal is intricate due to differences in data types, presentation, and reliability. Traditional approaches for achieving consistency rely on precise measurement calculation and clear models, but in many cases, data is subject to complex issues. Neural networks have shown potential in tackling inverse and ill-posed problems through direct data mapping, often producing accurate results. This research aims to develop an advanced data calibration method using a complex network of components. Each component in the network is configured using a pre-trained autoencoder to reduce data dimensions and an optimization module to ensure data consistency. Utilizing a dataset derived from various X-ray imaging systems, we demonstrate that this data calibration method can improve image quality, reduce artifacts, and enhance system reliability. This research has significant implications for medical imaging and promotes data sharing and interoperability across different radiology departments and modalities.

We investigate the algebra $\mathcal{Z}(C^*(G_\theta))$ of class functions in a quantum group, specifically the deformation of $SL_2(\mathbb{C})$, denoted as $G_\theta$. Our goal is to determine under what conditions the algebra of class functions becomes a maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra (MASA). Our analysis reveals that for deformations of $SU_q(2)$, the algebra of class functions is a MASA for all deformations. Conversely, for deformations of $SL_q(2)$, the algebra of class functions ceases to be a MASA once a certain deformation parameter exceeds a critical value. Our research sheds light on an anomaly in the MASA property and raises thought-provoking questions regarding the MASA property in quantum group algebras.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) with vast state or action sets often require approximations due to their size. In such cases, GMRES, an iterative method with finite-precision arithmetic, can be used to estimate the optimal policy for each approximate MDP. In this study, we examine the efficacy of inexact GMRES policy iteration (GMRA) and inexact projected GMRES policy iteration (PGMRAS) in relation to traditional policy iteration using MDP approximations via spectral grid refinement. We conduct experiments on large-scale MDPs in the case study category of Dyna-Q+. Results show that GMRES finds solutions of satisfactory quality with fewer iterations than traditional policy iteration. GMRES policy iteration is 100 times faster but yields results of lower quality, trading off precision for speed. Projected GMRES policy iteration is 800 times faster but produces estimates 10,000 times less accurate than GMRES policy iteration. Ineffectiveness of PGMRAS in our case studies may be attributed to the non-convex nature of the projection operation. Overall, while MDP approximations can enable efficient computation in large-scale problems, GMRES policy iteration and PGMRAS are not always equally effective due to potential loss in solution quality. The choice between them may be influenced by available computational resources and tolerance for long convergence periods.

We establish a relationship between the ordinary and symbolic powers of edge ideals of oriented graphs in the context of weighted graphs. Specifically, for weighted oriented graphs of a certain structure and characteristic zero, we demonstrate that for any positive integer $m$ and $s$, where $s$ is greater than the maximum weight among vertices in a graph, the symbolic power of the edge ideal equals the ordinary power of the edge ideal. Additionally, we prove a new relationship between the $m$-th symbolic power of an edge ideal and the coordinate vector of the vector $\vec{a} = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$. Furthermore, we determine under what conditions for vector $\vec{a}$ the symbolic power of the edge ideal is contained in the ordinary power of the edge ideal.

Optimizing a computer simulator is a crucial prerequisite for executing inverse problems with high precision, including calibrating the model and predicting unobserved outcomes. However, optimizing the simulator adds complexity and reduces efficiency as it necessitates multiple tunings and numerous simulations. To tackle this challenge, we suggest a novel approach that involves defining a policy to optimally configure the computer simulator based on current state information and predicted state. This method is then framed within a control theory context, where the policy is developed as the solution to a stochastic optimal control problem. Specifically, we apply the probabilistic variational approach to optimize the policy, which involves finding the best probability distribution parameter that minimizes the objective function. This framework allows for the separate optimization of each time step while maintaining computational efficiency through batch evaluations. Our framework's effectiveness and efficiency are validated through two case studies: one focusing on simulating turbulent fluid flows and the other on sampling from a simulator.

This research examines distribution-free robust learning within the context of metric spaces to understand how classifiable concepts respond to noisy data and classification functions. Our analysis centers on concept classes consisting of subsets in a metric space and focuses on two distinct scenarios based on the size of the concept class: one where the class is contained in balls and another where it contains balls. For classes containing balls, we discovered that even the simplest one-bit classification is challenging with a polynomial number of samples, given any query radius, with our sample complexity lower bound being exponential in the query radius. Conversely, given any query radius, we found that $e^{d^{*}}$ calls to a black box are sufficient for a randomized algorithm to achieve robust classification when the class consists of balls, where the exponential dependence on the query radius is an inherent property of robust learning, according to our analysis. Furthermore, we demonstrated that an algorithm can achieve distribution-free robust learning with nearly the minimal sample requirement of $O\left(\frac{\log |\mathcal{C}|}{\epsilon}\right)$ when the class consists of balls and we are allowed to use a query radius of $\epsilon$. In contrast, polynomial sample complexity is impossible for deterministic algorithms in non-compact metric spaces if query radii less than $\epsilon$ are used, with this requirement being independent of the class size and dependent only on the query radius.

The JESD algorithm, used for analyzing jet and isolated photon events, is capable of addressing background noise connected to photons that may not be significantly isolated. By incorporating a system that evaluates isolated photon candidates, it is possible to investigate the effects of photons on the structure of nearby jets. Data collected from proton-proton collisions with the ATLAS detector at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV are utilized for this purpose, focusing on events containing a high-energy jet and an isolated photon candidate in the range of 25-37 GeV. Observations indicate that when isolated photon candidates are present, the jet's initial conditions tend to be collimated and charge-imbalanced, whereas collimated and charge-imbalanced boson decays are more likely to result in photon candidates being discovered near jets.

Using the colored multiple zeta values expansion of $\pi$ and $\sqrt{2}$ provided in [2], 
we investigate Series 1.1.1 from "100 ways to $\pi$" and its alternating counterpart. 
We demonstrate that the parametric form of this representation involves only level 12 CMZV 
for the alternating series, in contrast to level 28 CMZV necessary for the non-alternating 
version; similarly, Series 1.1.2 and its alternating form require levels 16 and 25 
respectively. These evaluations also yield new representations for $\ell$ odd powers of $\pi$ 
and $\sqrt{2}$.

The primary process of a recent search led to the detection of a system featuring a brown dwarf and a distant, eccentric companion, LHS 5321 Cd. Analysis of available data indicates that Cd shares the same atmosphere as its brown dwarf parent, LHS 5321 C, with both exhibiting signs of K-type characteristics and similar effective temperatures of 2000-2100 K. It is hypothesized that Cd constitutes 3-10 times the Earth's mass, and may even be identical in mass to the Sun's natural satellite, the Moon. Furthermore, observational measurements of LHS 5321 C and Cd have also provided accurate measurements of their transverse distance and velocity, yielding a precision value for the system's habitable zone location, which is within 3-10 times the Earth's distance from the Sun.

This study会对 a long-standing hypothesis by Boal and Dasso's power law model be, which posits that all collision types obey a universal ratio pattern that declines with an increasing power of the scaled collision transverse area ($N_{\rm{coll}}/T_{\rm{nb}}^{\alpha}$). High-energy heavy-ion, proton-proton and proton-lepton collisions were examined for their prompt meson and baryon production in the central region. The data were collected by the ALICE detector at the CERN LHC in 2016. The results show that $N_{\rm{coll}}$ accurately accounts for the system-size dependence of prompt $\pi$, $p$, $\bar{p}$, $K$, $\bar{K}$, ${\rm{d}}$, and $\bar{{\rm{d}}}$ production across all measured systems, thus verifying the Boal-Dasso model for this purpose. The study also investigated the particle production characteristics in high-energy heavy-ion collisions during 2017 and observed that these particles exhibit distinct thermodynamic properties influenced by $N_{\rm{coll}}/T_{\rm{nb}}$. The observation that all collision types produce consistent particle spectra and flow is also reported.

Process calculations that involve parton-parton collisions, where multiple partons from a single incoming hadron collide, depend on double parton distribution functions (DPDs). These differ from standard parton distribution functions, as they account for the simultaneous presence of two partons within the same hadron. With the double parton scattering contribution to $K^+K^-$ production becoming accessible at future experiments like EIC and LHCb, our DPD-based calculations of this phenomenon will enable a double parton contribution assessment. Our calculations utilize various model DPDs and compare their outcomes to kinematic feasible regions extracted from existing data, focusing on the cross sections and momentum transfer values.

This study delves into the properties and potential applications of Martian and Lunar regolith glass, utilizing advanced techniques such as scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and thermal analysis to examine the material composition. Additionally, we investigated the manufacturing processes of Martian and Lunar glass, exploring the effectiveness of quenching methods using metal molds, water, and carbon dioxide gas. Our results reveal that Martian and Lunar glass exhibit similar structural and compositional characteristics to Earth glass, with significant implications for potential manufacturing and utilization in space environments.

The behaviour of a liquid film climbing a fibre is studied under the influence of gravity, focusing on the effects of varying slip conditions at the fibre-liquid interface. Our research reveals the emergence of unstable drops within the film under specific slip conditions, leading to periodic drop shapes with increasing frequencies as the slip at the fibre-liquid interface increases. By adjusting parameters such as slip, liquid-liquid surface tension, and liquid-structure interaction, we observe a continuous spectrum of periodic drop shapes. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression for determining the size of these drops, providing insights into their formation under different slip conditions.

The recent release of the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) Near Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) on the James Webb Space Telescope (James Webb Telescope) has opened numerous opportunities for (s)bfu research in both galaxy and high-z universe studies. Considering the upcoming depth surveys from JWST, researchers now face a significant challenge in efficiently selecting suitable targets for research. To address this issue, we have developed a $n^2$u research-optimized selection strategy for $n^2$u research-optimized deep-field (JWST) research, focusing on selecting optimal star-forming galaxy targets within multiple wavelength ranges. By combining (s)bfu model predictions of spectral energy distribution (SED) with empirical star formation rate (SFR) data, we can assess the accuracy of the SFR for the Prospector framework (Prospector). Results indicate that the $n^2$u research-optimized selection of UVCBGR (ultraviolet to near-infrared) targets can achieve a 90% success rate in detecting star-forming galaxies at z = 1-6 using 115-1150 Angstrom near-ultraviolet (nUV) to 1.6 micrometer (μm) photometry from JWST. Furthermore, the $n^2$u research-optimized selection strategy improves the accuracy of the SFR for Prospector to a 0.41 dex error margin

We take away the assumptions of unitarity and semi-simplicity from Cao-Lu-Kirillov exceptional structures. It is found that quadratic categories have Exceptional Braided Auto-Equivalences (EBAEs), which, upon semi-simplicity and unitarity, aligns perfectly with quadratic orientation data. Furthermore, it is established that EBAEs can decompose into basic building blocks called fundamental braided auto-equivalences. There is also a direct link between quadratic categories and gauge groups that define fundamental braided auto-equivalences. Finally, it is inferred that unitary categories' unitarity is a robust property.

We analyze the asymptotic behavior of the solution to the Fisher-KPP equation $u_t = \Delta u + u - u^2$ within a bounded domain with $u=0$ boundary conditions, given a non-negative, localized initial condition. The focus is on the regularity of the solution within the time frame where it hasn't been absorbed by the non-linearity. Although the solution maintains the support of the domain, we examine the smoothness of the solution within that region. With support in the $H^1$ norm, we investigate the behavior of the solution's second derivatives, denoted as $D^2u$. However, we discover that the non-linearity of the equation causes the availability of $D^2u$ to be more restricted than expected. As a result, the solution may cease to be differentiable in parts of the domain, even if it hasn't been completely absorbed. This phenomenon is supported by an explicit computation of the solution in 1D with a specific initial condition, and more generally, we establish the availability of the solution in the Healey-Pego-Pego $H^1$ framework with a more detailed analysis provided.

This paper outlines the methodology used for the SoundSCAPE entry in the UbiComp 2021 Challenge, a solution designed to detect written activities via wearable devices that detect audio but also capture space-related sound patterns. The goal was to determine if writing activities could be identified solely using audio sensors placed within a room. A two-pronged approach using machine learning techniques has been developed and tested in a controlled laboratory setting. First, written activities are detected using audio data, which is then utilized to identify walking routes via time-stamped data. Subsequently, a common mobile device is utilized to directly identify these routes, which are subsequently correlated with time-stamped audio data to confirm writing activities. Evaluation results on twenty subjects have yielded an overall accuracy of 85.5% in identifying writing actions.

The paper presents a novel approach to duration modeling, distinct from traditional methods that assume specific distribution characteristics, by employing a distribution-free approach. Instead, a conditional neural network model is developed to predict the median duration given an input sequence. This method is enhanced through the use of post-recursive neural network modules to capture uncertainty associated with duration conditions. Furthermore, a simple regression module is integrated to capture random variations resulting from inherent noise. Two strategies for condition encoding are proposed, involving either manual feature extraction or automatic feature learning through a neural encoding module. A multi-task learning approach is introduced, facilitating simultaneous modeling of the median duration, distributional uncertainty, and sequence length. An underlying neural network model is also proposed to capture duration quantiles using learned codebook representations.

Long-term ecological monitoring data collection often involves detecting species during predefined sessions, where absence is inferred from non-detection. However, traditional methods using frequentist likelihoods fail to incorporate monitoring absence data fully, while existing Bayesian methods make inefficient use of available data and slow modeling. To enhance occupancy model analysis, we present a new Bayesian approach, developed within the R2Bayes framework, that makes efficient use of detection absence data and accelerates model computation. Through simulated and real-world frog data, we demonstrate that our method yields comparable results to existing software, but with improved speed and efficiency, enabling ecologists to run ever-more-complex models in full Bayesian capacity.

This paper introduces the Skincare project, a collaborative venture between scholars and healthcare professionals including general practitioners and skin disease specialists. The Skincare project aims to construct a virtual diagnostic support system to assist professionals in evaluating and treating skin conditions with confidence and precision. We introduce a deep learning-based system for identifying and mapping skin lesions with high accuracy, combining the strengths of existing medical image analysis tools. To ensure reliable outcomes, we integrate multiple cutting-edge deep convolutional neural networks, create a custom ensemble of classifiers for lesion detection, and introduce a user-friendly software interface for clinical use. The Skincare project promotes seamless communication between skin disease researchers and medical practitioners, enabling access to advanced research results and analysis. We outline KPIs to measure and improve the Skincare platform, including evaluation metrics, output data, and user feedback from medical professionals.

Employing progenitor scenarios and explosion mechanisms that generate intrinsic variability in Type Ia supernovae, we aim to develop a cosmological model that accounts for their variable nature, resulting in a shift from the conventional dark energy paradigm to a more complex formulation of varied supernovae. As this involves both the parameters of cosmology and the parameters describing variability, we propose that the most efficient approach is through a penalty term that captures the connections between these parameters during the training process. Introducing this penalty term in our simulation-based training, a fully data-driven method that relies on lightcurves, we find that it enables us to capture the variability parameters effectively, resulting in improved likelihoods for our model. Furthermore, by testing our approach with simulated data, we find that the penalty term enables us to converge on the correct cosmological parameters, while excluding the variability parameters from contaminating our results. Ultimately, this research indicates that the most efficient method for capturing the variability of Type Ia supernovae in a heterogeneous ensemble is through the introduction of a correlation penalty term in the modeling and analysis of supernova lightcurves, ultimately resulting in a dynamic dark energy formulation.

Observations of gas dynamics in many galaxies are needed to understand how they evolve. We have obtained velocity maps of $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO molecular gas for the galaxy NGC 4478, a massive galaxy in the Virgo cluster, using the ALMA, VLA, and VLA+ESO-VLT array. We have also determined the total mass of outflowing gas and identified its origin. Although no significant gas mass loss is found, we found that about 44 percent of the gas in the inner 3 kiloparsecs of the galaxy is dynamically affected, likely due to outflows from the galaxy's inner region. These interactions could impact star formation within the region, as suggested by lower than expected star formation efficiency in the galaxy. We estimate that about 0.008 times the mass of the galaxy is lost through gas outflows annually in the galaxy. We have calculated other mass components and found that about 0.025 times the mass of the galaxy is falling onto the galaxy per year, while ionized gas mass losses are also present. We have further confirmed that the gas velocity dispersion in the galaxy correlates with its surface star formation rate, as expected in regions with active star formation, while velocity structures in the galaxy are driven by other processes on larger scales.

The interaction of particle-laden turbulent plumes with their environment has been an area of study, yet it has been largely unexplored when plumes exhibit negative buoyancy flux. Researchers conducted an experiment, sending plumes upward from nozzles of varying diameters into space, containing nozzles that allowed for an influx of particles of different sizes and densities. Data collection included parameters like particle distribution, plume size, and speed, facilitated by high-speed video and X-ray imaging. Results showed that plumes containing particles of a range of properties exhibited a comparable increase in size when their fluid properties promoted growth. Additionally, when particles within these plumes experienced a drag force and a balance with gravity, their presence led to an enhanced rate of plume growth.

In general graph-based models of contagion, where edges represent connections between vertices representing individuals, the models typically only consider the number of edges per node but not specifically which nodes are connected.  The Generalized contagion process is a stochastic model used to simulate the spread of infection, where the rate at which a node becomes infected depends on the number of infected neighboring nodes.  The rate of infection in a given model can be measured by the final number of infected nodes, known as the size of the outbreak, after the process reaches a steady state.  The size of the outbreak in processes governed by generalized contagion often exhibits a phase transition, where the outbreak size changes abruptly from remaining close to zero to significantly greater than zero.  The sudden change occurs when a critical threshold is reached, influencing the rate at which new infections are acquired.  We investigate how the size of an outbreak is affected by the regularity of graphs, where all nodes have the same degree but may not be connected to the same number of nodes.  We investigate two models: one where the degree of each node follows a Poisson distribution and the other where the degree of each node is randomly assigned from a uniform distribution.  It is revealed that the size of the outbreak is highly sensitive to changes in the rate of infection and the degree of regularity in both models.

Two-dimensional ferromagnetic bilayers exhibit controllable and strain-synchronized inverse topological semimetal characteristics, with their layer spacing affecting the topological properties. When compressed, the spinor texture transforms from a fully textured state at zero strain to a reverse textured state at a critical threshold of 0.02 strain, exhibiting gapped and antiferromagnetic properties in between. This phenomenon is attributed to the strain-induced exchange interaction that modifies the chemical potential and fillings within the multilayer structure, thereby regulating the half-metallic state's textural restoration.

Our research delves into the发生 mechanisms behind magnetic activity in stars. Previous studies demonstrated that magnetic fields can be amplified by stellar movement. However, magnetic fields can only be amplified, not determine the orientation of subsequent fields in these processes. A dynamic interaction with the star's differential rotation is necessary, with the star winding up a magnetic field during periods of quiescence until it triggers an activity cycle. We explored how magnetic fields behave in slowly rotating, late-type (K0M) stars and discovered two findings: Firstly, these stars can still exhibit magnetic fields despite their slow rotation due to their rapid equator-to-pole fluid flow. Secondly, these stars exhibit activity levels largely unaffected by their axial rotation period due to the lack of alignment with magnetic fields. These results, however, suggest an occurrence rate significantly lower than observed in more rapidly rotating stars, indicating an occurrence rate roughly 5-10% of the occurrence rate in rapidly rotating stars at intermediate latitudes.

We introduce a model that learns common features across multiple tasks and/or utilizes information from the outcomes of other tasks. The model employs a hierarchical structure with a prior distribution on entry levels to regulate how many features are shared. By using variational methods, we develop a contentful approach to estimate model parameters, enabling the discovery of redundant outputs. Numerical tests show the method's ability to enhance performance in both single-input and multiple-input scenarios, with applications to simulated data and image classification with text.

mc-3mfe is a specialized McMini version of the model checker designed to efficiently handle common multi-threaded operation definitions, such as those found in ANSI C11 and Java. By leveraging the 3-MFEO framework, mc-3mfe accurately models thread scheduling accuracy but also demonstrates a notable speed advantage, with an order of magnitude faster model checking process. Based on our strategy, we can establish an upper limit on the equivalence accuracy of three-thread operations defined within the 3-MFEO structure, which reveals that previous findings in model checking literature are complete under specific conditions. Additionally, we enhance existing results with new findings regarding thread scheduling accuracy.

Recently, misinformation has proven detrimental to society on a vast scale, necessitating practical approaches to curb its dissemination. Notably, WhatsApp has utilized advanced fact-checking technologies to tackle this challenge. By incorporating fact-checks into their messaging platform, WhatsApp has sought to provide users with reliable information and credible sources. To gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanism of this approach, we conducted an in-depth analysis of WhatsApp's "Official Fact-Check" feature. This study builds on our prior research into information flows within WhatsApp networks. Our findings involve conducting a large-scale experiment with 50K users, which enabled us to map out information propagation patterns and compare the impact of factual information with misinformation. We also investigated the effectiveness of highlighting the "Official Fact-Check" label on messages. Notably, we found that messages containing "Official Fact-Check" labels elicited significantly stronger responses from users. While our study's primary focus was on identifying key elements of the WhatsApp fact-checking mechanism, we believe its implications extend to exploring information dissemination within other social networks and systems as well.

This paper examines the evolutionary dynamics of a population divided into sub-populations, where mutations can occur and affect fitness. The population is modeled as a cluster of branching random walks with distinct traits that influence movement and reproduction. It's demonstrated that rare mutations lead to population fragmentation, with the number of sub-populations growing logarithmically as the population size decreases. Furthermore, it's found that the distribution of distances between populations follows an exponential pattern across different time frames. The results are validated through simulations with various population parameters.

For spoofing countermeasures, label propagation techniques have been widely used due to their efficiency in labeling, yet they're limited by the reliance on pre-defined boundary information, which can lead to propagation of inaccurate labels through propagation. In this research, we enhance the traditional LP method with attention mechanisms and non-local connectivity to improve speech artifact detection. The resulting method, referred to as Laplacian Attention Network (LAN), leverages neighboring information within a specified radius to update labels dynamically. The "attention" modules within LAN enable selective focus on crucial segments of input speech, while its multi-head structure enhances performance. Furthermore, LAN's incorporation of non-local modules optimizes long-range dependencies within a speech sequence, leading to superior outcomes. The experiment results on the AURAS and NIST-2015 datasets demonstrate LAN's ability to surpass the standards set by conventional LP methods and existing state-of-the-art spoofing detection algorithms.

We begin with a comprehensive summary of supergravity, establishing its links to quantum gravity, low-energy effective theories, and string theory. This serves as a comprehensive review to streamline specific derivations later on.

The integrity of the spin state of a single-atom source is heavily dependent on the coherence of the OAM states of the emitted photons. In order to assess the coherence of these photons, we conducted experiments on a silicon microdisk using a spatial light splitter and calculated the coherence between the $|\pm1|$ OAM states of the emitted photons. The results of the study revealed that the coherence functions of the photons increase as the pump propagation direction in the silicon disk is reversed. The study explains the phenomenon of pump direction dependence through the symmetry breaking of the optical mode coupling and provides insights into the polarization dependence of the spin OAM correlation of the emitted photons.

Optical properties of two specialized silicon materials, embedded silicon and buffer oxide silicon, have been investigated. By applying Hall compression and employing Hall effect measurements, it was discovered that embedded silicon contains significantly fewer carriers, less than 10 to the power of 15 per cubic centimeter, whereas buffer oxide silicon has a carrier concentration not exceeding 10 to the power of 13 per cubic centimeter,橙. Furthermore, it was observed that both types of oxide silicon exhibit intrinsic optical absorption at wavelengths greater than 1100 nanometers, whereas embedded silicon displays no optical absorption beyond 1150 nanometers. It is estimated that embedded silicon has a carrier concentration less than 10 to the power of 12 per cubic centimeter, whereas buffer oxide silicon has a carrier concentration less than 10 to the power of 10 per cubic centimeter.

A real number line partition is achieved by creating disjoint sets based on a property. 
We use this to demonstrate in a simple way that partitioning the line into Borel sets requires a higher cardinality than partitioning it into sets of closed numbers. 
This provides a simple proof that $2^{\mathfrak{c}}$ is necessary to divide the line into Borel sets. 
We also show the similar result for open sets and employ the argument to give a simple derivation that the power of the continuum, $\mathfrak{c}$, is equal to $2^{\omega}$.

This paper delves into the dynamics of short-term reversal trading within high-frequency stock trading environments, specifically focusing on the roles of Commodity Trading Advisors (CTAs). As CTA managers' short-term reversal trading strategies often lead to significant profits, this paper seeks to answer whether their interests align with those of reversal traders, or if their rewards come at the expense of CTA trading performance. We collect unique, private data from three prominent CTA trading firms, granting us insight into their short-term positional trades, including entry/exit times and strategy characteristics. By collaborating with behavioral finance experts who also engage in short-term reversal trading, we utilize sophisticated performance evaluation methods, such as Bayesian Kernel Regression Discovery, to analyze and compare their strategies in a mutually beneficial framework. Our analysis reveals that their short-term reversal trading has entry horizons spanning minutes to weeks, with profit-driven hold periods extending up to several weeks. Furthermore, we find that their interests and trading strategies are mutually beneficial, with expert entry times significantly enhancing the trading strategies of the CTA firms.

Evasion attacks against Dynamic Protocol Detection (DPD) are prevalent but their
impact is usually analyzed in the context of static signature matching. This work
takes a different approach, using a quantitative framework. We quantify the
efficiency of OpenWire, the industry standard for DPD, and its vulnerability to
attacks. Our results show that on average, 22.3% of random evasive payloads can
successfully hide their protocol and reach the server. Further analysis reveals
that attack vectors can be easily discovered and shared, allowing for an average
success rate of 19.2% when utilizing knowledge from existing attack vectors. To
mitigate this vulnerability, we propose and evaluate new DPD algorithms. Our
findings indicate that integrating randomness and record analysis can reduce
evasion success rates to under 5%.

Building upon previous research on magnetic strip arrays, we have built a dense strip of superconducting material integrated with a flat magnetic film. The presence of these superconducting strips, particularly their proximity to the magnetic film, creates an intricate pattern of external magnetic fields that interfere with magnon propagation, ultimately leading to the formation of standing waves of magnons. The types of these patterns are influenced by the spatial arrangement of the superconducting strips and the magnetic properties of the film. The integration of these systems also results in a weak coupling between magnons and photons, observed as changes in the transmission of microwave signals and the local changes in magnetic field distribution. The ability to precisely control this interaction makes magnon-photon systems a promising system to study interactions and light-magnon interactions.

Current approaches to training machine learning models across multiple decentralized devices face ongoing challenges in the federated learning context, particularly in navigating diverse data settings. A notable issue arises when trained models are applied to unseen data formats, resulting in decreased performance. To address this concern, we've developed a groundbreaking, unified framework that seamlessly integrates federated training and testing processes. By leveraging recent advancements in masked image modeling, our framework facilitates a sophisticated pre-training phase before transitioning to traditional federated learning. During the initial stage, our framework allows users to obtain high-quality global models trained on a broad range of global data types without requiring privacy-sensitive user input. Subsequently, in the federated training phase, users train local models on their individual input data and exchange only the model difference with the server, minimizing the disparity between local and global distributions as the phase progresses. During the final testing phase, our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on numerous benchmark datasets, surpassing existing methods in numerous instances, and highlighting the method's ability to accommodate a wide range of data types.

A crucial transformation in high-dimensional multi-photon systems is missing, which hinders their full potential in quantum computing, communication, and measurement. To make up for this shortcoming, we have developed a new method using linear optics and photonic integrated chips to perform a multi-dimensional Fourier transform on two photons. By combining our approach with other techniques, we can describe a complete, efficient group of transformations specific to multi-dimensional systems, which sets them apart from similar transformations available in quantum computing. Furthermore, our method offers the potential to utilize high-dimensional photons for speed increases in quantum algorithms, as well as enabling the use of linear optics with groups other than $Z_N$.
